title: AI chip shipments are about to jump an order of magnitude: from a million units to 15 million
dek: Broadcom's president lays out the AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with "beast" as the largest package at 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM, and four of the five frontier labs as partners.
why: Broadcom rarely discloses anything, yet here it gives three package tiers and three shipment tiers, plus a clear call on the HBM bottleneck; for anyone tracking ASICs and packaging, these 11 minutes carry more information than a lot of long analysis pieces.
who: Investors and chip engineers watching custom ASICs, advanced packaging and the HBM supply chain, plus founders trying to read the in-house chip moves at OpenAI/Anthropic.
skip: Anyone familiar with back-end design services can skip 0:01–2:07; the numbers are concentrated after 5:09.

points.h: Companies building their own chips still outsource the last step
points.body: Google, Meta, Amazon, and some frontier model companies can all have their own chip design teams, set their own architecture and interconnect, but in the end they still have to "get the thing built": deal with the foundry and the development kit, manage the timing and latency of the connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of the back-end design service providers that charge for this kind of work. Customers come to it not just for design capability but also for a batch of ready-made IP: high-speed I/O, high-speed compute, memory controllers.

points.h: The least talkative chip company suddenly starts talking about itself
points.body: Broadcom is a mystery externally: it has almost no PR department and rarely discloses anything on its own initiative. Occasionally it ships a Tomahawk networking chip, or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, president Charlie has unusually taken the stage at launch events to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it is expanding its customer base from traditional networking chips to custom AI chips. This slide showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

points.h: Today's AI servers are only the smallest of the three tiers
points.body: Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost one is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of the Cisco chip on the table: one compute die in the middle, four to six HBM around it, using a TSMC CoWoS-like package. Broadcom says that over the past year it has shipped more than a million of these chips for customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

points.h: The bigger the package, the higher the shipment volume
points.body: The middle tier is visibly larger: two to four compute/IO dies with eight to twelve HBM around them; AMD MI455X also counts as this design shape. The shipment expectations Charlie gave are the key: the middle tier is to ship 5 million units, and the rightmost tier is to ship 15 million. Set next to "a million units over the past year", this is not linear growth — it is next-generation custom AI chip shipments jumping a full order of magnitude.

points.h: The rightmost one may be compute die stacked on compute die
points.body: The rightmost beast: red is eight compute dies, arranged in two columns of four, and they are stacked. Charlie lifts the red to reveal purple underneath, which could be SRAM, or SRAM could be on top; if it is compute-on-compute, that is effectively sixteen compute dies. Each compute die gets two HBM, so one package holds sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue IO dies at the top and bottom ends, and openings left at the package edge for optical modules.

points.h: Nearly every frontier model company is building its own chip
points.body: Charlie said that of the five leading frontier model labs, four are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the design they want themselves, Broadcom does the back-end service and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn put it into data centers for deployment at scale. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it does not only serve traditional networking customers, it is also taking orders from large model companies.

points.h: What blocks the ramp may not be packaging but HBM
points.body: The real bottleneck may not be packaging but whether there is enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: will a new form factor outside HBM, sitting between DDR/LPDDR and HBM, emerge to fill the gap? Separately, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, a bit smaller than beast and closer in time. That is a reminder that over the next few years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will get swept up along with custom chip orders.

points.h: The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
points.body: The host pinned down that "coming soon, a bit smaller" 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George of Chips and Cheese, and the two concluded it is Fujitsu's Monaka — a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central IO die in between. This chip has already appeared at several conferences as a mockup or test silicon.

terms.def: The physical design stage after front-end chip design and before handing off to the foundry for production, covering place-and-route, timing closure and the like.
DRAM stacked directly adjacent to the compute chip through advanced packaging, with far higher bandwidth than ordinary DDR/LPDDR.
TSMC's 2.5D packaging process, placing multiple compute dies and HBM side by side on a silicon interposer.
A proprietary interconnect that links multiple accelerator chips into one logical large machine, distinct from ordinary data center networking.
